messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 34
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Parole Officer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 67

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Positive Feelings: push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe, Avoid Eye Contact: Making eye contact with other people, Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
  Threat: Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
  Negative Appraisals: Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kofi is a 34-year-old parole officer who has been with his girlfriend for three years, though the relationship has grown distant in recent months. Three years ago, his ex-partner, a woman he had lived with for two years, became violent during an argument. She pinned him against the wall, her forearm pressed across his throat; he could smell the antiseptic hand sanitizer she had just used at her nursing job. She screamed that he was worthless, that no one would ever believe him. He remembers the taste of blood from his bitten lip, and even now, when the memory returns, he can taste that metallic saltiness as though it were fresh. The sound of her voice—the exact pitch and rhythm of her threats—sometimes plays in his head without warning, and the memory does not feel like something from the past; it feels as though he is back in that moment, pinned and helpless, his airway closing.

Kofi works in a downtown parole office, where he meets with formerly incarcerated men in a small, windowless room. The smell of the building’s industrial disinfectant hits him every time he walks through the door, and his body immediately goes on alert. His shoulders tighten, his jaw clenches, and he begins scanning the hallway for any man who might be standing too close or looking at him too long. He watches their hands, their posture, their eyes. When a parolee holds his gaze a second longer than expected, Kofi feels the memory surge—the taste of blood, the sound of her voice—and he becomes convinced that the man is about to attack. What happened to Kofi was deeply unfair, he believes, and nothing has been done about it; his ex-partner faced no consequences, and he has come to feel that his life has been destroyed by what she did. There are days when he is not sure his life is worth living anymore.

These appraisals drive much of Kofi’s behavior. Because he believes his life is already ruined, he has stopped pushing back against small provocations at work. He avoids any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation, even when a parolee is clearly violating a condition of release. He has also begun avoiding eye contact with everyone—colleagues, strangers, his girlfriend—because looking someone in the eye feels like an invitation to be seen, and being seen feels dangerous. He pushes away positive emotions, too: when his girlfriend tries to hold his hand or tell him she loves him, he pulls back, because feeling good feels unsafe, as though any moment of softness will be punished.

The constant threat monitoring feeds back into itself. Kofi’s body is perpetually tense, ready to react, and this hypervigilance means he notices every potential danger—a man walking behind him in the parking lot, a stranger’s lingering glance. Each perceived threat triggers the memory again, and each memory reinforces his belief that the world is unsafe and that his life has been stolen. His avoidance strategies, in turn, make the memories more intrusive: by dodging eye contact and conflict, he never tests whether his fears are realistic, so the memory retains its power to feel present and real. And by avoiding positive feelings, he starves himself of any experience that might counter his negative appraisals.

The cycle tightened over months. Kofi began arriving late to work, claiming traffic, because the antiseptic smell in the lobby was unbearable. He stopped attending team meetings, citing caseload pressure, because sitting in a room full of men made his skin crawl. His supervisor noticed his avoidance of conflict and assigned him fewer high-risk cases, which Kofi interpreted as proof that he was failing. At home, his girlfriend stopped reaching for him; she told him he felt like a stranger. What finally brought Kofi to seek help was a moment in the parole office when a client—a large man with a quiet voice—said, “You okay, man?” and Kofi froze, tasted blood in his mouth, and could not speak for nearly a minute. He realized he could no longer do his job. He is afraid that therapy will not work, that he is too broken, but he is also afraid of what will happen if he does not try.
